column1: The EU defence budget is now $10bn (£3.4bn; $4.2bn), it added on Tuesday, a fact which has caused consternation and concern among EU leaders who believe that Europe's existing supply of weapons is inadequate and can be used by Russia.
The announcement came after it emerged that the EU had agreed to add $50m to its security budget.
EU defence ministers are due to meet in Brussels on Thursday and EU heads of state, diplomats, civil servants, civil servants of all political parties will be invited to discuss the matter.

A separate memorandum of understanding, the second of which was signed last week, allows EU states "to provide for a single, uniform, unified system of defence, defence-related programmes as well as specific requirements for defence production and production".

That means it will be possible to supply more than 50 million rounds of ammunition, which had been estimated to last to two years and could be used by the Ukrainian army as "military ammunition" by the end of the year.
But the EU has a long way to go before that happens.
For instance, it could not provide supplies to the Russian army until the end of the year. That has not happened yet.
The EU has been trying to reach a deal with Russia as part of a broader deal to reduce tensions over Ukraine.
And it is understood that the EU has already offered a £3.4bn (£2.1bn) contribution to Ukraine's defence industry which would be used to provide defence equipment and training for Russia.
But the EU is still unclear on how much of the funding it is offering Russia will be used to improve defence equipment. And it could be the money that is used by Ukraine to help support its defence.
The EU is also under pressure to provide extra support to the Russian military.

If this is done, it is not very likely that there will be a significant reduction in the level of armed conflict in the Russian-Ukrainian border.
